# Results — Study 517 (Pre-FOMC-Drift)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — Lucca &
Moench (2015): **a large fraction of the equity premium is earned in the ~24 hours before a
scheduled FOMC announcement**. We hardcode the scheduled-FOMC announcement calendar, tag the
SPY trading session that ends just before each meeting, and compare its return to every other
day — over the full sample, split at the **2012** post-publication era, and decomposed into
overnight vs intraday. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to
reproduce every number. Fingerprint `9687074d1493`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes (SPY) + raw SPY Open/Close + a 30-name survivor basket (public, no key) |
| Window | 1993-02-01 → **2026-05-29** (**33.3** years; 8,389 daily SPY returns) · as-of 2026-05-31 (last complete month) |
| FOMC calendar | **261** scheduled announcement dates, **hardcoded** (Federal Reserve 1994–2026); **260** map onto pre-FOMC sessions in the price tape |
| Pre-FOMC days | **3.1%** of all sessions (the session ending just before each scheduled announcement) |
| Decay split | full-sample, then **pre-2012** vs **post-2012** (Lucca-Moench circulated 2011, published 2015) |
| Timing / costs | pre-known calendar (no look-ahead); timing rule pays **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per meeting |

> **Survivorship (named on the Signal axis).** SPY itself is survivorship-clean (an index ETF),
> so the *headline* pre-FOMC test does not carry the bias. The cross-sectional basket of 30
> names *still trading* in 2026 does — a fixed surviving-names panel tilts up — so we keep the
> basket as colour and lean the verdict on the survivorship-clean SPY tape.

## The signal — pre-FOMC day vs all other days (SPY close-to-close, full sample)

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| pre-FOMC mean return | **+0.227% / day** (one-sample *t* = **3.04**) |
| other-day mean return | +0.042% / day |
| Welch *t* (pre-FOMC − other) | **+2.44** |
| share of **total** cumulative return on **3.1%** of days | **14.7%** |
| placebo *p* (random 260-day calendars ≥ observed mean) | **0.007** |

Read it carefully. On the **full** 33-year tape the pre-FOMC drift is real and large: those
**3.1%** of sessions carry **14.7%** of SPY's entire cumulative return, the pre-FOMC mean is
**+0.227%/day** (≈5× the other-day mean), the one-sample *t* is **3.04**, the two-sample Welch
*t* is **2.44**, and a 20,000-draw random-calendar placebo puts *p* = **0.007**. This clears the
desk's **t ≥ 2** bar and survives the placebo — the Lucca-Moench effect is genuinely on the tape.

## The decay — it is a pre-publication museum piece

Lucca & Moench circulated the finding in 2011 and published in 2015. Split the sample at 2012:

| era | pre-FOMC mean | other-day mean | Welch *t* | share of cumulative return | n pre-FOMC days |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **pre-2012** | **+0.335% / day** | +0.028% / day | **+2.94** | **27.4%** | 145 |
| **post-2012** | +0.091% / day | +0.061% / day | **+0.28** | 4.7% | 115 |

The whole signal lived **before** the paper. Pre-2012, the pre-FOMC day earned **+0.335%/day**
(Welch *t* = 2.94) and **27.4%** of all cumulative return sat on 3% of days. Post-2012 the
pre-FOMC day is **+0.091%/day** versus +0.061% for every other day — a Welch *t* of **0.28**,
statistically indistinguishable from a normal session. This is textbook McLean-Pontiff decay:
the edge was arbitraged away once it was public.

## Overnight vs intraday — is it the run-up into 14:15? (the third axis)

Lucca-Moench tell a story about equities drifting up *into* the early-afternoon statement, which
would put the return in the **intraday** session. Decompose SPY's pre-FOMC return into the
overnight gap (prior close → open) and the intraday session (open → close), full sample:

| component | pre-FOMC mean | other-day mean | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| overnight (prev close → open) | +0.108% | +0.030% | +1.70 |
| intraday (open → close) | +0.120% | +0.005% | +1.78 |
| daily (close → close) | +0.227% | +0.035% | +2.54 |

The pre-FOMC excess is split **roughly evenly** between the overnight gap (+0.108% vs +0.030%)
and the intraday session (+0.120% vs +0.005%) — neither component alone clears *t* = 2, and only
the **combined** close-to-close return does. So the popular "it's all the morning run-up into the
release" framing is **only half right**: a meaningful chunk arrives overnight before the session
even opens. The clean single-session story is **Mixed**, not confirmed.

## Tradability — the gross edge survives costs, but the decay kills deployment

A calendar rule that holds SPY only on pre-FOMC days is two trades per meeting on a deep, liquid
ETF, so costs are nearly free:

| one-way cost | gross pre-FOMC mean | net pre-FOMC mean | net one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.5 bp | +0.227% | +0.217% | 2.91 |
| 1.0 bp | +0.227% | +0.207% | 2.77 |
| 2.0 bp | +0.227% | +0.187% | 2.51 |

Costs are **not** the binding constraint here — SPY is liquid enough that 1–2 bp barely dents the
edge (net *t* stays ~2.5–2.9 on the full sample). The thing that makes it un-deployable is the
**decay**: the post-2012 Welch *t* of **0.28** means a trader starting today would be timing a
dead signal. The edge is real in the archive and gone in the present.

## Robustness — tag the session strictly before the announcement

The headline tags the announcement-day session itself (the statement lands intraday). As a strict
no-look-ahead variant, tag the session **strictly before** the announcement date (`shift = −1`):

| variant | pre-FOMC mean | Welch *t* | share of cumulative return |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| announcement-day session (headline) | +0.227% | +2.44 | 14.7% |
| strictly prior session (`shift = −1`) | +0.161% | +1.40 | 10.4% |

Shifting the window back a day **weakens** it (Welch *t* drops to 1.40): the drift is concentrated
in the session that *ends* at the release, exactly as the announcement-run-up story predicts. The
effect is timing-sensitive — another reason it is fragile to harvest.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful (seed-averaged)

On a deterministic daily world with a *planted* pre-meeting drift, the pre-vs-other test behaves
exactly as it must — averaged over **40 RNG seeds** (no single-lucky-seed claim):

| planted edge | mean Welch *t* | fraction of seeds with \|*t*\| > 2 |
|---|--:|--:|
| **0.00%** (no edge) | **−0.09** | **0.05** |
| **+0.40%** (large planted drift) | **+4.24** | **0.97** |

With **no** planted drift the test sits at *t* ≈ 0 with a 5% false-positive rate (exactly nominal
— noise cannot fake it); a large planted drift lights up with 97% power. The measurement is
unbiased, so the real-tape full-sample *t* = 3.04 is a genuine signal, not a construction artefact.

## Verdict

- **Signal — REAL.** On the full 33-year tape the pre-FOMC session earns **+0.227%/day**
  (one-sample *t* = **3.04**, Welch *t* = **2.44**, placebo *p* = **0.007**) and **3.1%** of days
  carry **14.7%** of SPY's cumulative return — clearing the desk's **t ≥ 2** bar, surviving a
  random-calendar placebo, and confirmed faithful by a seed-averaged synthetic control. The
  Lucca-Moench drift genuinely existed. REAL, not WEAK.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Costs barely touch the edge on liquid SPY, but the signal **decayed
  to nothing post-publication** (post-2012 Welch *t* = **0.28**, indistinguishable from a normal
  day), and it is timing-sensitive (shifting the window one day back drops *t* to 1.40). Real in
  the archive, dead in the present — not INVESTABLE.
- **"It's the run-up into 14:15"? — MIXED.** The pre-FOMC excess splits **roughly evenly** between
  the overnight gap (+0.108% vs +0.030%) and the intraday session (+0.120% vs +0.005%); neither
  component alone clears *t* = 2, only the combined day does. The "all morning run-up" framing is
  only half the story — a meaningful slice arrives overnight before the open.
